overview:
It began with a quarrel over religious guarantees in Bohemia and ended thirty years later as a continent-wide contest over Habsburg power. In May 1618 Protestant nobles in Prague threw the emperor's representatives out of a castle window, elected Frederick V of the Palatinate as their king, and set about besieging Catholic strongholds such as Pilsen. Ferdinand II crushed the revolt at the White Mountain in 1620, but the settlement he imposed — confiscations, forced conversions, a redrawn electoral college — alarmed princes far beyond Bohemia and drew in outside powers one after another. Christian IV of Denmark intervened and was beaten at Lutter in 1626. Sweden's Gustavus Adolphus landed in 1630, broke the imperial army at Breitenfeld in 1631 and at Rain on the Lech in 1632, and was killed later that year at Lützen in a battle his side nonetheless won. When the Swedes were shattered at Nördlingen in 1634, France abandoned the pretence of merely subsidising the emperor's enemies and entered openly in 1635 — Catholic France funding and fighting alongside Lutheran Sweden, which is the clearest sign that confession alone never explained the war.

The last thirteen years were the grinding ones. Armies criss-crossed the Empire living off the land under a system of contributions that amounted to organised extortion, and the fighting spread outward: a Dutch fleet destroyed a Spanish armada in the Downs off the English coast in 1639, French forces bled the Bavarians at Freiburg in 1644, Swedish armies won again at Breitenfeld in 1642 and smashed the imperial field army at Jankau in Bohemia in 1645. By 1648 the emperor could no longer defend his own capital-in-Bohemia: Swedish troops scaled the walls of Prague's Malá Strana in July, took the castle and shipped Rudolf II's art collections down the Elbe, and were still being held off at the Charles Bridge by the townspeople when news of peace arrived. In the same summer the French crushed a Spanish army at Lens. Negotiations had by then been running for years in the Westphalian towns of Münster and Osnabrück, and the treaties signed on 24 October 1648 confirmed what the battlefield had settled — Sweden took Western Pomerania and Bremen-Verden, Brandenburg and France made gains, Calvinism was recognised alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, subjects were no longer bound to their ruler's faith, and Dutch and Swiss independence was acknowledged.

What the war cost is genuinely contested. Older accounts of a Germany depopulated by a third rest on tax and parish records that are patchy and easy to misread; current estimates usually run between roughly four and a half and eight million dead across three decades, most of them from hunger and epidemic disease rather than combat, with ruin distributed very unevenly — Magdeburg was annihilated in 1631 while other regions were barely touched. The Franco-Spanish war that had become entangled with it did not stop in 1648 and ground on until 1659, a reminder that the tidy dates are a convenience.
significance: The war permanently weakened the idea that the Holy Roman Emperor could govern Germany as a single Catholic monarchy, leaving several hundred princes with real freedom of action and making Brandenburg-Prussia, Bavaria, Sweden and above all France the powers that would shape Europe for the next century. It also left the settlement of 1648 as a founding reference point for how states deal with each other: a peace negotiated by multilateral congress rather than dictated by a victor, with confessional loyalty formally detached from political allegiance. International-relations theory later built the whole doctrine of "Westphalian sovereignty" on those treaties, though historians now regard that as a nineteenth- and twentieth-century back-projection — the treaties themselves kept the Empire's overlapping jurisdictions intact and were far less revolutionary than the label suggests. The more durable legacy may be the memory of the devastation itself, which fixed in German culture a sense of catastrophe that later invasions were measured against.
coverage: Written from general reference works — the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, World History Encyclopedia, and the Peace of Westphalia article — rather than from the specialist literature or archival demography, so the population and casualty figures here are ranges taken on trust from a debate this summary cannot adjudicate. The hundred events in this dataset are almost entirely battles and sieges, which skews the story toward campaigns and commanders; the diplomacy, the contributions system that paid for the armies, and the experience of civilians and of the soldiers' vast camp followings are barely represented, and the surviving record for the latter is thin and heavily mediated by clerical and official sources.
